intro: Mahler’s country dancers have heavy shoes, and his waltzers have sharp elbows. Three dances share the second movement of the Ninth, until the orchestra leaves only a piccolo and a contrabassoon to pick up the pieces.

sections.label: A · A clumsy C-major Ländler
sections.mNote: Bassoons and violas introduce the fiddling second violins

sections.label: B · A quicker waltz in E major
sections.mNote: The strings change pace but keep three beats

sections.label: C · A gentler dance in F major
sections.mNote: Falling seconds and spacious phrases slow the dance

sections.label: B′ · The waltz returns in D major
sections.mNote: The quicker tune returns with new turns and sharper accents

sections.label: A′ · The Ländler for solo strings
sections.mNote: Viola, cello and violin recover the first dance

sections.label: B″ · The waltz pushes back in
sections.mNote: Brass and strings make the faster dance rougher

sections.label: A″ · The Ländler comes apart
sections.mNote: The opening figures scatter between winds and strings

cues.title: Fiddles in heavy shoes
cues.text: Bassoons and violas offer a quick upbeat, and the clarinets answer. The second violins bring in the Ländler, a country dance. Mahler marks the page Etwas täppisch und sehr derb — somewhat clumsy and very coarse — and asks the violins to play wie Fiedeln, like fiddles.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, Universal Edition first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 59: Im Tempo eines gemächlichen Ländlers, Etwas täppisch und sehr derb; bassoons and violas with the upbeat figure; second violins marked Schwerfällig and wie Fiedeln. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has the clarinet gesture introduce the movement, the melody marked etwas täppisch und sehr derb and the violins schwerfällig, wie Fiedeln: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The waltz elbows in
cues.text: The tempo suddenly quickens — Poco più mosso subito (Tempo II) — and a waltz elbows in, louder and weighted on the downbeat, in four sharps. The sigh-shaped melodic lines of the first movement are still there, but chromaticism and dissonance grow.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 64–65: Poco più mosso subito (Tempo II), four sharps, ff accents in the strings. Basinger: as the first dance fades the tempo suddenly increases and the Austro-German waltz intrudes with a significant increase in volume and a switch to downbeat emphasis; sigh-shaped lines remain while chromaticism and dissonance grow: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fish sermon, quoted
cues.text: The movement quotes the scherzo of Mahler’s Second Symphony, his orchestral version of St Anthony’s sermon to the fish, for a few bars among the dances.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide records a brief reference to the Second Symphony’s “Fischpredigt” (its third movement, an instrumental version of the Knaben Wunderhorn poem) in this movement, at the start of the coda: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

cues.title: A trial in rehearsal
cues.text: Fred Gaisberg later admitted that rehearsing this Ländler movement for the recording was a time-consuming trial. He had arranged five rehearsals before the concert so that his engineers could test their equipment.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay quotes Gaisberg’s proposal of five rehearsals for tests and experiments and reports his 1947 confession about rehearsing the Ländler: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: A slower pair of feet
cues.text: After a long Molto riten. a solo bassoon leads into Tempo III (Ländler, ganz langsam), a very slow dance. The sigh figures of the faster dances are still in it, but at this pace, with a triangle added, the mood lightens.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 73: Molto riten., Tempo III (Ländler, ganz langsam), bassoon marked Solo. Basinger: the slow Ländler shares an ascending bass line and sigh figures with its predecessor, and the reduced speed and the triangle lighten the atmosphere: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The waltz spins faster
cues.text: The waltz returns, reharmonized and varied. At rehearsal 22 the key signature is two sharps, the strings alternate plucked and bowed notes, and the woodwinds add little turns to the tune.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 77, rehearsal 22: two sharps, pizzicato and arco alternating in the strings, turn figures in oboes and clarinets. Basinger: the slow Ländler bookends restatements of the Austro-German waltz, which Mahler has reharmonized and varied melodically: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three Ninths in Vienna
cues.text: At the Vienna festival in June 1912, Walter introduces Mahler’s Ninth alongside two older Ninths: Beethoven’s, conducted by Felix Weingartner, and Bruckner’s, under Arthur Nikisch. Three conductors take on three very different endings.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, p. 1, documents the three Ninths at the Vienna Music Festival Week and their conductors. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: A dance for fewer players
cues.text: Two bassoons quietly recover the opening upbeat. The old Ländler now belongs to a solo second violin and a solo viola, with the other violas plucking beneath. Its heavy shoes have become much easier to lift.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 86: two bassoons with the upbeat figure, 2. Violine Solo and Viola Solo, violas pizzicato. Basinger: Mahler abbreviates the return of the moderate Ländler: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Seventy minutes
cues.text: Walter’s performance lasts about seventy minutes, close to the “hour and thirteen minutes actual playing length” of the première in 1912 and eleven minutes brisker than his own stereo recording of 1961.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay gives about 70 minutes for the 1938 performance, 81 minutes for Walter’s 1961 Columbia recording and Gaisberg’s figure for the première: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: The dancers lose the tune
cues.text: The first tempo returns abruptly and the Ländler resumes with uncharacteristically heavy accents. They soon lighten, and the dance begins to come apart in fragments.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the Austro-German waltz returns etwas frischer; an abrupt restoration of the original tempo feels discordant, the moderate Ländler resumes with uncharacteristically heavy accents, and these soon lighten: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

cues.title: “The dance is over”
cues.text: Bruno Walter wrote of this movement in 1936: “A tragic undertone sounds in the joy and one feels that ‘the dance is over’.”
cues.evidence: Walter’s Gustav Mahler (1936), quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: The dance slips away
cues.text: In the coda, muted sounds and a pianissimo give the music a mischievous air. Fleeting fragments of the Ländler emerge and sneak away, instrument by instrument.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: at first muted timbres and a pianissimo create a mischievous atmosphere; then fleeting fragments of the moderate Ländler emerge and sneak out, instrument by instrument: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

cues.title: Piccolo meets contrabassoon
cues.text: At opposite ends of the orchestra, piccolo and contrabassoon share the opening upbeat, under the marking Nicht eilen bis zum Schluss — don’t hurry to the end. The dance has dwindled to this improbable pair. Plucked strings supply the last small punctuation.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 103: Nicht eilen bis zum Schluß, piccolo and contrabassoon figures at pp, a solo viola, a final pizzicato chord in the strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The waltz arrives suddenly
transitions.to: B · A quicker waltz in E major
transitions.how: The first Ländler begins to fade. Then, at Poco più mosso subito (Tempo II), the tempo quickens and the waltz intrudes, louder and weighted on the downbeat, with a new key signature of four sharps.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 64–65: Poco più mosso subito (Tempo II), four sharps. Basinger: the tempo suddenly increases and the waltz intrudes, with a switch to downbeat emphasis.

transitions.title: A bassoon upbeat slows the dance
transitions.from: B · A quicker waltz in E major
transitions.to: C · A gentler dance in F major
transitions.how: A long Molto riten. slows the waltz almost to a stop. A solo bassoon leads into Tempo III (Ländler, ganz langsam), a very slow dance that keeps the sigh figures of the faster ones.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 73: Molto riten., Tempo III (Ländler, ganz langsam), bassoon Solo. Basinger: the slow Ländler shares sigh figures with its predecessor.

transitions.title: The waltz gathers from little scraps
transitions.from: C · A gentler dance in F major
transitions.to: B′ · The waltz returns in D major
transitions.how: The slow Ländler gives way to the waltz again, reharmonized and varied. By rehearsal 22 the key signature is two sharps, the strings alternate plucked and bowed notes and the woodwinds add little turns.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 77, rehearsal 22. Basinger: the slow Ländler bookends restatements of the Austro-German waltz, reharmonized and varied.

transitions.title: Two bassoons recover the beginning
transitions.from: B′ · The waltz returns in D major
transitions.to: A′ · The Ländler for solo strings
transitions.how: The slow dance fades. Two bassoons quietly bring back the opening upbeat, and the Ländler returns in a solo second violin and a solo viola, with the other violas plucking.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 86: bassoons, 2. Violine Solo, Viola Solo, violas pizzicato. Basinger: an abbreviated return of the moderate Ländler.

transitions.title: The first tempo comes back
transitions.from: B″ · The waltz pushes back in
transitions.how: The waltz is marked etwas frischer, somewhat brisker, and then the first tempo abruptly returns. The Ländler resumes with heavy accents, which soon lighten.
transitions.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the Austro-German waltz returns etwas frischer, the original tempo is abruptly restored and the moderate Ländler resumes with heavy accents: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement II, printed pp. 59–103: bassoon, viola and clarinet opening; three dances at Tempo I, II and III; piccolo and contrabassoon in the final bars.

timeline.note: Bassoons and violas give the upbeat; clarinets answer on three square beats.
Second violins play the coarse Ländler tune like fiddles.
The strings bring in the quicker waltz at Tempo II.
Horn and strings give the slower dance its gently falling phrases.
Viola, cello and solo violin recover the first Ländler.
Brass and strings make the returning waltz heavier and rougher.
Woodwinds and strings exchange scraps of the dance.
Piccolo and contrabassoon share the upbeat; upper strings end with a plucked note.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Commons, the surviving concert-programme catalogue and the Library of Congress essay agree on orchestra and conductor.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The recording sources identify the complete movement but do not establish the performing edition or any local alterations. The 1912 full score is used as a structural reference, not proof of the parts on the 1938 desks.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: 16 January is the documented public concert date. Pristine gives 15–16 January 1938 for its reissue; the inspected evidence does not establish whether any rehearsal material entered the issued matrices. The Commons embedded “1962” digitising tag is not accepted as a performance or transfer date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The concert-programme catalogue names the hall and city; Commons uses Musikvereinsaal de Vienne.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names only an unspecified audio CD. HMV made the original 78-rpm issue, but the CD label used for this upload has not been identified.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The source CD catalogue number is unknown. Pristine documents the historical ten-disc HMV set as DB 8569–8578; that does not identify the carrier transferred for Commons.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Pristine lists the original complete-set matrix series 2VH 7027–7046. The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The embedded digitising value 1962 is not corroborated as a transfer date and is not used as one; neither upload nor release dates substitute for it.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Commons supplies an Ogg Vorbis file and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: Embedded metadata names Xiph.Org libVorbis I 20100325 (Everywhere). The original 1938 performance was cut on alternating wax-recording machines, but the intervening CD restoration, equalisation, edits and mastering are not identified for this file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mahler died in 1911. This is a term calculation for the composition, not worldwide clearance of an unidentified edition or transfer.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the sound recording.
fields.note: The inspected template expressly concerns expired performer and producer rights in the European Union. This package is admitted on that territorial recording-rights basis, not merely the composition’s age. United States status is not established; no worldwide public-domain clearance is asserted.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
